tldr: To solve the problem of legged robots shutting down from motor overheating long before the battery runs out, this paper proposes a reinforcement learning method that penalizes predicted steady-state "asymptotic temperatures" calculated instantly from per-gait-cycle torques and speeds. Without ever observing temperature, the policy dramatically extends continuous walking time under a 5 kg payload from 19 minutes to 174 minutes (running the battery completely flat).
hero_caption: Comparison of walking at 1 m/s carrying a 5 kg payload. The baseline policy (top) concentrates heat on specific motors and suffers a thermal shutdown in just 19 minutes. In contrast, the proposed policy (middle) keeps walking for 174 minutes until the battery is fully depleted, with a 14 °C margin below the thermal threshold on its hottest motor.
overview:
Reinforcement learning has drastically improved the traversal capabilities of quadruped robots, raising expectations for sustained tasks such as payload transport and facility inspection. In the real world, however, robots hit an annoying wall: long before the battery is empty, specific joint motors overheat, triggering an emergency thermal shutdown. Joule heating—the primary heat source in permanent magnet synchronous motors (PMSMs)—scales quadratically with torque, meaning load concentration on a few joints drives them to critical temperatures in no time.

Existing countermeasures include adding hardware like fans or liquid cooling, but they add weight and draw power. On the software side, incorporating motor temperatures directly into the reinforcement learning reward makes credit assignment extremely difficult: thermal time constants (tens of minutes) are orders of magnitude longer than reinforcement learning steps (a few seconds), so the policy cannot tell which actions caused the temperature rise. Furthermore, feeding current temperatures to the policy as observations causes it to adopt an overly timid posture even when motors are still cold, crippling its ability to climb stairs and other rough terrain.

To overcome this, the authors took a counterintuitive approach: stop observing temperature altogether. Under a sustained gait, the equilibrium temperatures (asymptotic temperatures) the motors will eventually settle at can be computed instantaneously from the gait-averaged squared torques and joint speeds of just a single cycle, simply by solving a system of linear equations from a compact thermal network. By penalizing the maximum (softmax) of these asymptotic temperatures, the policy naturally learns walking patterns that distribute heat away from hot joints—all without any temperature input.

In real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2, under a 5 kg payload walking at 1 m/s, the learned baseline reached thermal shutdown after 19 minutes (1.1 km), whereas the proposed policy ran for 174 minutes (10.0 km) until the battery was completely drained. It also completed an unloaded factory circuit with stairs and ramps without sacrificing traversal capabilities, successfully shifting the robot's operating limit from temperature to battery.
contributions: Proposed a reinforcement learning reward that solves for steady-state asymptotic temperatures from per-gait-cycle squared torques and joint speeds and minimizes their softmax, distributing thermal load without ever observing temperature.

Constructed a 13-node thermal RC network by pre-identifying physical electrical power balances (idle power, Joule heating, and copper temperature coefficient), achieving a mean RMSE below 1 °C on unseen data while preserving physical consistency.

Demonstrated on a physical Unitree Go2 that continuous walking time under a 5 kg payload extended from 19 minutes to 174 minutes (until battery depletion), while maintaining high traversal capabilities on a demanding factory circuit with stairs and ramps.

sections.heading: Why robots stop from heat long before the battery dies
sections.summary: Although reinforcement learning has greatly enhanced quadruped agility, real-world operation is often cut short by motor overheating. The thermal challenge is a distribution problem governed by the single hottest joint rather than total energy minimization, and learning is hindered because thermal time constants vastly outlast the RL credit assignment horizon.
sections.details:
Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) have endowed legged robots with remarkable agility. However, during sustained tasks such as payload delivery or facility patrols, motor thermal protection triggers (around 86 °C on the Unitree Go2) and stops the robot while plenty of battery charge remains.

This problem is challenging for two main reasons:
- **Difference from energy minimization (distribution problem)**: Robot shutdown is not decided by the total energy consumed across all joints, but by the single hottest joint. Even if a gait has high overall energy efficiency, concentrated torque on specific joints (such as the knees or hips) causes rapid overheating.
- **Difference in time constants (credit assignment difficulty)**: Motor temperatures change over tens of minutes. In contrast, the Joule heating that causes it is generated instantaneously by the current squared torque. If raw temperature is used as a reward in a short RL episode (a few seconds to tens of seconds), the policy cannot discern which action drove the heat increase because temperature barely moves during that window.

Previous studies attempted to provide motor temperatures as observations to the policy or used Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) on temperature rate-of-change as rewards. However, these methods induced overly timid postures from the start when motors were cold, making the robot incapable of traversing obstacles like stairs and ramps.

The authors therefore propose to observe no temperatures at all. Under steady-state walking, the equilibrium temperatures (asymptotic temperatures) that motors will settle at are uniquely and algebraically determined from the squared torques and speeds of a single gait cycle via a thermal model. By driving down these asymptotic temperatures through rewards, the long thermal time constant is compressed into the short timescale of a single gait cycle (about 1 second), successfully spreading heat without temperature inputs.

sections.heading: Physics-based thermal identification and asymptotic temperature rewards
sections.summary: A 13-node thermal RC network was identified from two robot runs under electrical power-balance constraints. From this model, steady-state temperatures (asymptotic temperatures) are computed linearly from single-gait-cycle torques and speeds, and RL is trained with a reward minimizing their softmax.
sections.details:
The core of this method lies in identifying an accurate thermal model and instantaneously deriving asymptotic temperatures from it to construct an RL reward.

### II-A Thermal system identification
First, the authors built a 13-node lumped RC thermal network (12 joint motors plus the base body) describing heat conduction and dissipation across the robot. The state equation is:
$$\mathbf{C} \dot{T} = P(u, a, T) - \mathbf{G}_a(v)(T - T_a\mathbf{1}) - \mathbf{L} T$$
where $\mathbf{C}$ is the heat capacity matrix, $u_j = 	au_j^2$ is squared torque, $a_j = |\dot{q}_j|$ is joint speed, $\mathbf{G}_a(v)$ is ambient dissipation conductance dependent on air speed (walking velocity $v$), and $\mathbf{L}$ is the graph Laplacian representing inter-node conduction.

Fitting curves purely on temperature data causes thermal capacitances and resistances to collapse into physically implausible values, degrading generalization. To prevent this, the authors leveraged the robot's total power balance (bus power $P_{\mathrm{bus}} = V|I|$). Total idle power $p_{\mathrm{idle}}^{\mathrm{tot}}$ was directly determined from static and resting phases, and linear least squares was applied to static and walking power data to fix the Joule heating coefficient $k_m$ and copper temperature coefficient $\alpha$. A two-stage identification approach was used, solving for only the remaining 19 parameters via nonlinear optimization. Data collection required just two real-robot runs (Protocol A: unloaded speed sweeps and posture shifts; Protocol B: 5 kg payload and center-of-mass shifts) totaling about 4 hours.

### II-B Steady-state-aware thermal rewards
During sustained walking, high-frequency torque fluctuations are attenuated by more than 2000 times due to the low-pass filter characteristics of the thermal network. Thus, setting $\dot{T} = 0$ with gait-averaged squared torques $ ar{u}$ and speeds $ ar{a}$, the settling asymptotic temperature $T_{\mathrm{ss}}$ is obtained instantaneously by solving a compact $13 	imes 13$ linear system:
$$(\mathbf{G}_a(v^{\mathrm{cmd}}) + \mathbf{L} - \mathbf{J}_{T}( ar{u})) T_{\mathrm{ss}} = P_0( ar{u},  ar{a}) + \mathbf{G}_a(v^{\mathrm{cmd}}) T_a \mathbf{1}$$
This matrix inversion completes on the microsecond scale and can be evaluated at every environment step during RL training. Because heat capacity $\mathbf{C}$ vanishes at steady state, $T_{\mathrm{ss}}$ is entirely independent of transient response parameters.

The resulting joint asymptotic temperatures are normalized to $[40, 80]$ °C, and the reward $r_{\mathrm{ss}}$ is defined using a power mean (softmax with $p=20$):
$$r_{\mathrm{ss}} = - \left(  rac{1}{12} \sum_{j=1}^{12} (T_{\mathrm{ss}, j}^*)^{20} ight)^{1/20}$$
Setting $p=20$ focuses the penalty on the hottest joint while providing smooth gradients across the policy. While a naive temperature variance penalty can be exploited by intentionally heating cold joints to reduce variance, this maximum-suppression formulation is immune to such hacking.

### II-C Baselines and our thermal policy
Blind locomotion policies (without external cameras) were trained using PPO in Isaac Lab across diverse terrains, including stairs up to 20 cm and ramps. From the baseline (DreamWaQ) reward, redundant terms—electrical power variance, joint mechanical power, and base height tracking—were removed, and the asymptotic thermal reward (weight $w_{\mathrm{th}} = -0.2$) was added. Because standing tall with straighter knees naturally reduces torque and lowers asymptotic temperature, enforcing a target base height is no longer needed.

sections.heading: Outstanding continuous endurance proven in simulation and on hardware
sections.summary: The identified model showed remarkable accuracy with a mean RMSE below 1 °C across 21 unseen runs. After verifying thermal margins and terrain traversal in simulation, physical robot experiments demonstrated sustained locomotion of 174 minutes (10.0 km) with a 5 kg payload and 47 laps (11.2 km) on a factory circuit, running until battery depletion without thermal shutdown.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluated thermal model prediction accuracy, simulated locomotion and terrain traversal, and real-world endurance limits.

### III-A Thermal system identification
The thermal model was validated across 21 test runs (totaling 39 hours) never seen during identification, involving a different Go2 robot instance, different controllers, payloads up to 10 kg, and speeds up to 1.4 m/s. The model achieved a mean RMSE below 1.0 °C across all 12 joints, and under 1.25 °C for peak temperature predictions on the most critical joints.
In an ablation study where electrical power balance constraints were removed and all 22 parameters were fitted purely to temperature data, idle power was estimated at 18 W (versus the measured 44 W), drifting far from physical truth and clearly degrading generalization error on unseen data.

### III-B Gait evaluation in simulation
Flat-ground walking at 1 m/s (payloads 0–5 kg) was evaluated in simulation. For the baseline, the maximum asymptotic temperature reached $91 \pm 8$ °C even with no load, and surged to $131 \pm 14$ °C at 5 kg payload, vastly exceeding safe thresholds. In contrast, the proposed policy kept temperatures around 72 °C at 5 kg with $w_{\mathrm{th}} = -0.2$, and around 67 °C with $-0.3$, securing substantial thermal margins.

### III-C Terrain traversal in simulation
To confirm that thermal awareness did not compromise agility, policies were tested on stairs up to 20 cm and steep ramps. The proposed policy ($w_{\mathrm{th}} = -0.2$) reduced endpoint tracking error on uphill climbs by 20.2 %, incurred only a minimal increase in stair velocity error (0.02–0.03 m/s), and maintained a high survival rate exceeding 99.7 % (no falls).

### III-D Endurance on flat ground
A physical Go2 carrying a 5 kg payload walked continuously on flat ground at 1 m/s. The baseline overheated its rear motors and shut down after only 19 minutes (1.1 km). In contrast, the proposed policy walked for **174 minutes (10.0 km)** until the battery reached zero percent. At shutdown, its hottest motor was 72 °C, maintaining a 14 °C margin below the 86 °C threshold. Reduced Joule heating lowered total power draw from 244 W to 142 W (a 42 % reduction) and improved the Cost of Transport (CoT) by 43 %, from 1.24 to 0.71.

### III-E Factory circuit
Next, an unloaded endurance test was conducted on a 239 m factory circuit featuring 19.5 cm stair risers, ramps, and sharp turns. While the baseline suffered thermal shutdown after 25 laps (6.2 km, 111 minutes), the proposed policy completed **47 laps (11.2 km, 193 minutes)** on a single battery charge. The peak joint temperature saturated at 64 °C (a 22 °C margin), and CoT was reduced by 34 % from 1.27 to 0.83.

captions.F4: Maximum asymptotic temperatures across payload weights. Compared to the baseline (off-chart) and a heavy torque-squared penalty policy (orange), the proposed policies (green and blue) show very mild temperature rises as payload increases, matching the low temperatures observed on the physical robot (green crosses).
captions.F6: The factory circuit used in real-robot experiments. Despite steep stair climbs, narrow corridors, downward ramps, and sharp turns, the robot under the proposed policy traversed the circuit stably without losing balance.
captions.F7: Peak joint temperature over time on the factory circuit. The baseline (purple) hit the 86 °C shutdown threshold at 111 minutes, whereas the proposed policy (green) saw its temperature saturate near 64 °C, sustaining operation until battery depletion at 193 minutes.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: This work demonstrates that penalizing asymptotic temperatures derived from a thermal RC network turns legged locomotion limits from thermal shutdowns to battery depletion, all without observing raw temperatures. Future work includes closing sim-to-real gaps at high payloads and dynamically adjusting commanded speeds via the thermal model.
sections.details:
This study fundamentally resolves motor overheating—the primary bottleneck limiting the sustained range and endurance of quadruped robots—purely through control design.

The key insight is penalizing the future thermal steady state (asymptotic temperature) of the current gait rather than current temperature, which barely moves during an episode. This bypasses the credit assignment problem in reinforcement learning and enables the policy to spontaneously learn heat-spreading gaits without requiring temperature sensor feedback.

Hardware experiments on the Go2 extended sustained walking under a 5 kg payload from 19 to 174 minutes (over a 9-fold increase) and demonstrated robust performance on a demanding factory circuit with stairs and ramps until the battery ran flat.

Three directions are highlighted for future work:
- Reducing the small sim-to-real temperature discrepancy observed under high payload conditions
- Integrating an electrical power minimization reward using the power balance already embedded in the thermal model to turn thermal headroom into additional travel range
- Implementing an autonomous thermal governor that dynamically dials back commanded walking speed ahead of overheating based on real-time thermal model predictions

sections.heading: Appendix: 13-node thermal network equations and parameter identification details
sections.summary: Defines thermal balance equations for each actuator node and the hidden base node, alongside a first-order lag model for temperature sensors. It also details the identification procedure that determines Joule heating coefficients and temperature coefficients from static and walking power balances.
sections.details:
The appendix provides detailed mathematical formulations and identification steps omitted from the main text.

### Appendix A Full node-level equations
Each joint actuator node $j$ receives Joule heating $P_j^J$, viscous friction losses $f a_j$, and idle power $p_{\mathrm{idle}}$. Considering the bypass conductance $\varphi_y$ to the base, it conducts heat with neighboring nodes $\mathcal{N}(j)$ and dissipates heat to the ambient air (natural convection conductance $g^a$, forced convection from walking wind $c_v v^n$, and rear-leg wind-shielding factor $s_{\mathrm{rear}}$). The base node $B$ receives idle compute power $p_{\mathrm{idle}}^B$ and bypass heat from the joints, dissipating heat to the environment. Measured motor temperature $\hat{T}_j$ tracks the actual node temperature $T_j$ via a first-order lag with time constant $	au_m$.

### Appendix B Identified thermal and electrical parameters
The identification procedure first fixes total idle power $p_{\mathrm{idle}}^{\mathrm{tot}} = 44.0$ W from the average bus power during resting (damp) phases. Next, Joule heating power—derived by subtracting mechanical power from total power across 15 static and walking segments—was fitted via linear least squares to yield the Joule heating coefficient $k_m = 0.494$ W/(N m)$^2$. The copper temperature coefficient $\alpha$ was fixed to the physical value of copper, $3.93 \cdot 10^{-3}$ K$^{-1}$. The remaining 19 thermal parameters were determined in seconds by nonlinear least squares (Trust-Region Reflective algorithm) minimizing temperature residuals across the two runs (~19k samples). Reflecting the physical construction of the Go2, where thigh and calf motors sit adjacent to each other, the identification confirmed that thermal conductance between calf and thigh nodes was the most dominant conductive pathway.

takeaways: When addressing slow physical phenomena like temperature in RL, computing steady-state asymptotes analytically from algebraic equations and using them as rewards is a powerful way to solve the credit assignment problem.
For sustained legged robot endurance, naive total energy minimization is insufficient; minimizing the maximum temperature across joints (via a softmax penalty) is essential.

In thermal system identification, anchoring model scales with electrical power balances (e.g., bus power) alongside temperature curve fitting is crucial for achieving both physical consistency and high generalization.
limitations: A sim-to-real gap remains under 5 kg payload walking, where physical asymptotic temperatures were about 4.6 °C higher than simulation predictions.
The thermal network must be identified once per robot model (Unitree Go2 in this study); robots with different actuator layouts or mechanical structures require dedicated data collection.
The current implementation lacks an active thermal governor to automatically reduce commanded velocity, which may become necessary under extreme ambient temperatures or even heavier payloads.
